problem: VLA navigation policies need large robot datasets that are costly to collect. Egocentric human walking videos are abundant, but human viewpoint jitter and human-versus-robot motion differences make them hard to use directly for mobile robot imitation learning.
motivation: Human egocentric video is cheap and scalable, and it has already been used to augment manipulation datasets. Navigation is harder because the camera moves during locomotion, so human trajectories must be converted into actions that fit ground-robot kinematics before they can serve as supervision.
key_idea: Estimate camera motion from egocentric walking videos with monocular visual odometry (SuperPoint + LightGlue + essential matrix), project it onto planar nonholonomic motion, smooth and discretize it into robot actions, then co-train a VLA on these pseudo-labelled human data plus real robot demonstrations.
insight: Human-only training fails (0-22% success) because of the camera and motion domain gap, and robot-only training breaks under distractors and unseen starts. The co-trained model gets the best of both: distractor success rises from 22.2% to 88.9-94.4%, and unseen-start success rises from 41.7% to 75.0%. Human data appears to add language grounding, since the co-trained model handles non-training targets (green apple, orange), and diverse motion, while robot data anchors the action distribution. There is no ablation of the pipeline components (filters, thresholds) or of the mixing ratio.
method: Visual motion estimation: monocular VO using SuperPoint keypoints, LightGlue matching, and RANSAC essential-matrix decomposition, with frame-to-frame poses accumulated into a trajectory.

Kinematic projection: relative SE(3) pose is projected to SE(2), with forward velocity from translation along the forward axis and yaw rate from the planar rotation. Scale ambiguity means translation is treated as a normalized 'motion intention' signal, not a metric speed.
Velocity clipping, median filter (N=5) and constant-velocity Kalman filter (Q=0.005, R=0.5) to smooth the velocities; clip limits are v ±0.3 and ω ±0.5.

Action discretization: threshold rules (τ_fwd=0.3, τ_bwd=-1.5, τ_turn=0.003) map velocities to forward/backward at 0.2 m/s and turns at the robot's nominal rate, followed by a mode filter that removes transitions shorter than 12 frames.

VLA model: frozen SigLIP2 + DINOv3 dual encoder with linear feature fusion, an 8-layer Transformer adapter (language queries attend to visual keys/values), and an 8-layer DiT action expert trained with conditional flow matching to predict a 32-step action chunk.

Co-training: human-derived image-action pairs and robot-collected demonstrations are combined in one dataset. Robot data covers the camera and dynamics gap; human data adds diversity and language variety.

setting.backbone: SigLIP2-base-256 + DINOv3 ViT-B/16 (frozen) with a trained 8-layer Transformer adapter and 8-layer DiT flow-matching action expert
setting.training_data: 150 real robot trials (red apple only; 50 per goal) plus 80 human egocentric trials recorded on an iPhone (all 3 fruits; the text also says 240 videos in total) converted to image-action pairs
setting.observation: monocular RGB from a fixed front camera (480x640, 30 fps) plus a language instruction and robot state
setting.action_space: discrete forward/backward/turn/stop commands (0.2 m/s linear, 0.4 rad/s angular), predicted as 32-step chunks

numbers.extra: human-derived + robot data; 2 trials per start-goal combination

Ours (co-training) — orange, no distractors / with distractors

numbers.eval_set_note: unseen starts S_E, S_F; red apple only, no distractors; 2 trials per combination

numbers_note: Custom real-robot fruit-search task, not a standard benchmark. Baselines are robot-only (unseen starts 41.7%; trained starts 88.9 NoD / 22.2 Dist) and human-only (unseen 0.0%; 5.56-22.2 on trained starts).
results: Co-training reaches 88.9-100% success from trained starts without distractors and 88.9-94.4% with distractors, versus robot-only 88.9% and 22.2%. On unseen starts it achieves 75.0% versus 41.7% for robot-only and 0% for human-only. Human-only data alone fails almost entirely.
limitations: Still requires robot-collected data to bridge the domain gap; the mixing ratio and the amount of robot data needed are not studied.
Very small evaluation (2 trials per combination, single lab environment, one 2-DoF robot), and no ablation of the pipeline components or of the discretization thresholds.
Monocular VO has scale ambiguity, so only coarse discrete intent actions are recovered; quality depends on the recorder's motion and on video coverage.
